newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Biodiesel producers seek EU Commission support.
newsitem.headline: Biodiesel producers seek EU Commission support.

text.p: Biodiesel producers in Europe are seeking EU Commission help to overcome a looming raw materials shortage, Werner Koerbitz of the Austrian Biofuels Institute (ABI) said on Friday.

"We want the Commission to create a sound basis for renewable crops on environmental grounds and to make the EU less dependent on imported fossil fuels," he said in an interview during the Lipidex 97 oilseeds fair.
"Biodiesel is derived from domestic oilseeds and this raw materials base is threatened now the EU has cut the percentage of land for set-aside to five percent," he said.
He was on his way to a Commission hearing in Brussels later on Friday at which he planned to present future scenarios for the role biodiesel might play in transport applications.
"I will say that we need to ensure the industry can carry on, it can't operate on a stop and go basis," Koerbitz said.
The EU in 1996 produced 550,000 tonnes of biodiesel and was due to make 639,000 in 1997, with France, Italy and Germany accounting for the largest shares of the total in that order.
But the industrial oilseeds area for the 1997 harvest is expected to fall sharply along with the halving of set-aside.

The 1992 transatlantic Blair House accord not only limits the EU oilseeds area for food production, it also caps the volume permitted for growing oilseeds for industrial use at one million tonnes of soymeal equivalent.
Koerbitz told the conference the technical refinement and environmental advantages of biodiesel meant its use had now been endorsed by many of the world's leading car manufacturers.
The fuel does not pose a threat to traditional car petrols because its market share is minute at well below one percent.

It produces less greenhouse gases -- such as carbon dioxide and less sulphur and soot -- than petrochemicals products. It can reduce global and local pollution and the damaging effects of global warming and acid pollution.
Biofuel is non-toxic, has high biodegradability, and waste oils such as used frying oil can easily be recycled. Higher biofuels use would create additional jobs in Europe.

Supporters want the EU to implement a plan by which 12 percent of the European consumption of transport fuels in 2020 (pegged at 370 million tonnes after 270 million tonnes in 1995) would be covered by biofuels such as rapeseed, cottonseed and tallow "diesel."
They argue there will be greater use for alternative fuels as fossil fuel resources are declining, energy demand in Asia is growing dramatically, and North Sea oil may be exhausted by 2010.

They say increased land resources will be supplied by the integration of 10 eastern European countries into the EU which will add 55 percent to the total arable area. Industrial crops cultivation would curb the possible emergence of new food crop surpluses in these countries.
Koerbitz also said he had assurances from German plant breeders that rapeseed oil yields could be raised from 1.40 tonnes per hectare in 1997 to 2.90 tph by the year 2020.
The ABI is an organisation of independent scientists who act as consultants on biodiesel and bioethanol facilities.
